pages.title: Text back every missed call automatically for an HVAC business
pages.summary: When a call is missed during a job, send an automatic text asking for the address and issue, log the reply, and alert the on-call tech.
steps: Connect your business phone system (a VoIP service such as OpenPhone, Dialpad or a Twilio number) so it fires a webhook or Zapier trigger on missed calls.
In Zapier, Make or n8n, send an SMS: “Sorry we missed you — this is {Company}. Reply with your address and the issue (no heat / no cool / maintenance) and we'll call back within the hour.”
Log every reply to your CRM or a Google Sheet.
Forward the reply to the on-call technician's phone.

pages.title: Alert staff when a SKU drops below your reorder threshold
pages.summary: Watch an inventory sheet or POS export; when a SKU falls below the threshold you set, alert staff and optionally draft a supplier reorder email for approval.
steps: Keep live stock counts in a Google Sheet (or export SKUs nightly from your POS into one).
Add a reorder_threshold column per SKU and a supplier email column if you want drafted emails.
In n8n, Zapier or Make, schedule a check that finds rows where quantity is at or below the threshold.
Send a Slack/email alert to staff with SKU, quantity, and threshold.
Optionally draft a supplier email (do not auto-send until a human approves) listing items to reorder.

p: Tools: Google Sheets or POS export + n8n/Zapier/Make + email or Slack. Inventory-below-threshold alerts are a common small-business automation pattern (see https://useomniai.com/n8n-automation-ideas-small-business/).

This is different from a restaurant inventory-variance alert (usage vs sales). Here you only care that on-hand quantity crossed a reorder line.
Don't auto-order from suppliers without a human check — bad counts create bad POs.
Tune thresholds after a week or two so you aren't flooded with false alerts.

pages.summary: Type your offer, end date and code as real text near the top of promo emails instead of baking them into one graphic. Outlook blocks downloaded pictures by default, Apple Mail and Gmail can show AI summaries, and screen readers can't read words inside an image.

p: More people see your deal: shoppers whose email app hides images, people skimming an AI-written preview on their phone, and customers who use a screen reader.

Gmail can show an AI Overview at the top of an email that sums up its key points.
Email agency Backstroke says these AI summaries work from an email's live text, so an offer that appears only inside an image can be left out of the summary.
The W3C's accessibility guidelines say to use real text instead of pictures of text, and that when an image does contain text, its alt text should repeat the same words.

ol: Open your last promo email in your email tool's preview with images turned off. Can you still tell what the offer is, when it ends and how to redeem it?

Keep your graphic as decoration. If it has words in it, give it alt text with the same words.
Make your main button a real text button in your email editor, not a picture of a button.
Put the offer in the subject line and preview text too.
Send a test to yourself on an iPhone and in Gmail, and check that the preview or summary mentions the offer.

ul: AI summaries can get things wrong, and you can't control what they say. Clear, short text at the top is your best bet.
Put exclusions and fine print in real text as well, so nobody misses them.

pages.summary: Pull this year's payments to non-employees from your bookkeeping tool, flag anyone you'll likely need to send a 1099-NEC to, and send each one a secure W-9 request with automatic reminders until it's on file. steps: Export this year's payments to contractors and other non-employees from QuickBooks, Xero or your bank: payee name, email, total paid so far, and whether you already have a W-9 on file.

For each flagged payee with no W-9 on file, have Zapier, Make or n8n send a short email asking them to upload the current IRS Form W-9 through a secure upload link (your accounting software's vendor portal, a secure form tool, or your accountant's client portal). Never ask for the form or a Social Security number by plain email reply.

When a W-9 arrives, the upload tool's "new file" trigger marks the row "received" and stops the reminders. Someone on your team checks that the name and taxpayer ID box are filled in and the form is signed.
Send up to two reminders a week apart, then put anyone still missing on a call list for the owner or bookkeeper.
In early January, hand the finished sheet to your bookkeeper or accountant, or use it to file through the IRS's free IRIS portal.

p: Tools: your bookkeeping software, Google Sheets, Zapier/Make/n8n, your email tool, and a secure file-upload or client-portal tool. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page. No AI step is needed. If you use one to write the reminder email, give it the payee's first name only.

blocks.h: Dates and numbers to know (checked at IRS.gov)
ul: For payments made in 2026, you report non-employee pay on Form 1099-NEC when it totals $2,000 or more for the year. For payments made before 2026 the threshold was $600, and the IRS says it will be adjusted for inflation after 2026.

Form 1099-NEC is due to both the IRS and the payee by January 31. When that falls on a weekend the deadline moves to the next business day, and January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, so the 2026 forms are due Monday, February 1, 2027.
If a payee doesn't give you a correct taxpayer ID, the IRS says you may have to hold back 24% of future payments (backup withholding).
If you file 10 or more information returns in total, you have to e-file. The IRS IRIS Taxpayer Portal is free and lets you upload a .csv file.
A W-9 contains a Social Security or taxpayer ID number. Keep it out of email threads, chat tools and AI tools. Store it in one access-controlled place.
Collect W-9s before you pay new contractors next year, so this becomes a one-time step per vendor.
Who counts as a contractor and which payments are reportable can be tricky. This recipe only gathers the paperwork; your accountant decides what gets filed.

Food Code adoption is up to each state and local health department, so check your local rules.

For each release the team says: "There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice."
Linux distributions and long-term support vendors got the patches in advance, so many hosts can update quickly.
PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates from the PHP project. PHP 8.2 gets security fixes only until December 31, 2026.

ol: Find out if your site uses PHP. If it's WordPress, it does. In WordPress, go to Tools > Site Health > Info > Server to see the PHP version; the Status tab flags an outdated PHP version as a security issue.

If you're on PHP 8.2, ask about moving up before it reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

Some hosts patch PHP in the background with their own builds, so the version number may look different. Ask them to confirm in writing that these two CVEs are fixed.

pages.seoTitle: Stop payment-change email scams: an automatic verify-before-pay hold
pages.summary: Scammers send emails that look like they're from a vendor, landlord or even the owner, asking you to pay to a "new" bank account. This recipe flags any email that mentions changed payment details, puts the payment on hold, and reminds staff to call the sender at a number you already have on file before a single dollar moves. The FBI and FTC both recommend this kind of second-channel check.
steps: Make a simple vendor contact sheet (Google Sheets or Airtable) with each vendor's known phone number, taken from a contract or past invoice, not from a new email.

In Gmail or Outlook, or with Zapier, Make or n8n, set a rule that flags incoming email containing phrases like "new bank account", "updated wire instructions", "change of payment details", "ACH change" or "pay to this account instead".

When a message is flagged, add a row to a "Payment change holds" sheet (sender, vendor, date, amount if stated) and send the owner or bookkeeper an alert that says: HOLD. Call the vendor at the number on file before changing anything.
Optionally, have an AI step summarize what the email is asking for in one line. It should never reply to the sender or click links in the message.
Staff call the number from the vendor sheet, confirm the change with a person they recognize, and record who they spoke with and when. Only then does the bookkeeper update the payee details.
Send yourself a weekly list of open holds so nothing gets paid, or stuck, by accident.
Write down what to do if money already went out: call your bank right away to ask for a recall of the funds, then file a complaint at ic3.gov.

p: Tools: your email (Gmail or Outlook rules), Google Sheets or Airtable, and optionally Zapier/Make/n8n for alerts. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

blocks.h: What the FBI and FTC recommend
ul: The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) recommends using secondary channels or two-factor authentication to verify requests for changes in account information.

IC3 also suggests checking that the sender's address and any links really match the business they claim to be from, watching for misspelled domain names, and never sending logins or personal information by email.
If you discover a fraudulent transfer, IC3 says time is of the essence: contact your financial institution immediately to request a recall, and file a complaint at ic3.gov regardless of the amount.

The FTC tells small businesses to put verification policies in place, for example requiring employees to call and confirm wire transfer requests they receive by email, and to use a phone number you know is correct rather than the one in the message.
The FTC also recommends email authentication (SPF, DKIM and DMARC) on your own domain so scammers have a harder time sending email that looks like it came from you.
Never call the phone number or click the link inside the suspicious email. Use the number from your own records.
Keyword rules miss some scams. Train staff that any request to change where money goes gets a call, flagged or not.
Don't let an AI tool reply to, forward or act on these emails automatically. It only flags and summarizes.
Ask your bank what fraud and recall help it offers before you need it.

Put the offer in your Small Business Saturday and Cyber Week plans so it shows up before and during Thanksgiving week.
Track gift card sales each week so you know what's working, and plan for redemptions in January and February.

ul: Follow the federal gift card rules: funds generally must be good for at least five years, and fees must be clearly disclosed. Simplest is no fees and no expiration.
Don't promise package details you can't deliver on busy dates. State any blackout dates up front.
Gift cards are a liability until they're redeemed. Ask your accountant how to record them.
Survey figures describe national shopper plans. Your own sales may differ, so start small and watch the numbers.

blocks.h: Protect your gift cards from card draining
p: Card draining is a gift card scam aimed at generic gift cards hanging on open racks at grocery stores, pharmacies and big-box stores. A thief takes a card off the rack, scratches or peels the cover to copy the card number and PIN (or puts a fake barcode sticker over the real one), reseals it and puts it back. When a shopper buys the card and loads money on it, the thief spends the balance online, often before the gift is ever opened.
ul: If you sell your own gift cards: this is a strong reason to sell direct. Offer e-gift cards from your own website, and keep physical cards behind the counter so they're only activated at your register when someone pays.
Keep any physical cards you sell out of open, self-serve racks. If a reseller stocks your cards, ask how they store and protect them.
Tell your customers the safest way to buy is straight from you, in person or on your website. It protects them and keeps the sale with your business.

Buyer tips: buy direct from the business or online from the brand's own site. In a store, check the back of the card for torn, wrinkled or resealed packaging, a scratched or exposed PIN, or a barcode sticker, and pick a different card if anything looks off.
Keep the receipt and a photo of the card. Register the card if the issuer allows it, check the balance right away, and give the gift soon so it's used before anyone else can drain it.
If a card has no money on it, contact the card issuer and the store where you bought it right away. Paying by credit card can give you more ways to get your money back.

steps: List every domain you own and every website on it in a Google Sheet: domain, registrar, renewal date, whether auto-renew is on, the card on file, and who has the login.

Log in to your registrar, turn on auto-renew for every domain you want to keep, and make sure the card and contact email are current. ICANN requires registrars to send renewal reminders about a month and a week before expiry, so those emails must reach an inbox someone reads.
Ask your web host or website builder whether your certificate renews automatically. Most hosts and builders do this for you; if yours doesn't, ask them to set it up.

ul: The CA/Browser Forum's Ballot SC-081v3 cut the maximum lifetime of public website certificates to 200 days for certificates issued on or after March 15, 2026, then 100 days from March 15, 2027 and 47 days from March 15, 2029.

ICANN's Expired Registration Recovery Policy requires registrars of generic domains (like .com) to send at least two reminders before expiry, about one month and one week ahead, and another within five days after it expires.
Don't rely on renewal emails alone. An old address, a full inbox or a spam filter means nobody sees them.

p: Reviews that stay up, and a Business Profile that keeps collecting new ones through the holidays, instead of reviews that get removed or a warning on your listing during your busiest season.

ul: Google's Maps contribution policy says merchants may not offer incentives, such as payment, discounts, free goods or services, in exchange for posting a review, or for changing or removing a negative one.

The same policy says merchants may not discourage negative reviews or selectively ask only happy customers for positive ones, and shouldn't pressure customers to review while they're on the premises or ask for specific wording.
Google says reviews posted because of an incentive are not allowed and will be removed.

If Google finds a business broke its Fake Engagement policy, it may, beyond removing reviews, block new reviews for a set time, unpublish existing reviews for a set time, or show customers a warning that fake reviews were removed. Google says it emails the owner first, and owners can appeal.

ol: Read through your holiday plans: social giveaways, Small Business Saturday offers, receipts, table cards, email footers and staff scripts. Remove anything that links a review to a prize, entry, discount or freebie.

Ask every customer the same way, not just the ones who seem happy. A short line on the receipt or in a follow-up email with your Google review link works (see the review-request recipe).

pages.summary: Holiday hiring moves fast, and paperwork is easy to miss. steps: Keep one Google Sheet of new hires: name, start date (first day of work for pay), manager, and checkboxes for I-9 Section 1, I-9 Section 2, W-4 and any state forms.

Have the automation work out the Section 2 due date (3 business days after the start date) and write it into the sheet.

ul: The employer or an authorized representative must complete and sign Section 2 within 3 business days of the hire date, meaning the first day of work for pay. USCIS's example: someone who starts Monday needs Section 2 done by Thursday.
If the job lasts less than 3 days, Section 2 must be completed no later than the first day of work for pay.

The employee chooses which acceptable documents to present: one from List A, or one from List B plus one from List C. If they present acceptable List A documentation, don't ask for List B or C, and vice versa.
Employers must physically examine original documents, unless they participate in E-Verify and use the remote alternative procedure that DHS authorizes.
Employees can't act as the authorized representative for their own Form I-9, and the employer is liable for violations by any authorized representative.
Never tell a new hire which specific document to bring, such as a passport. Send them the full USCIS list and let them choose.
Count business days, not calendar days, and use the first day of paid work, including paid training or orientation.

Treat the reminders as a checklist, not a compliance program. For special cases like minors, rehires or reverification, see the USCIS Handbook for Employers (M-274), and ask an employment professional if you're unsure.

pages.summary: Some scammers flood a Google Business Profile with 1- and 2-star reviews, then message the owner offering to remove them for money, gift cards or free services. Google says don't engage and don't pay: paying encourages more attempts and doesn't guarantee removal. Save the evidence and report it through Google's merchant extortion form.

p: A clear plan for the day it happens, so you protect your rating and your money instead of negotiating with a scammer during a busy season.

ul: Google calls review extortion a serious policy violation. It may look like a sudden increase in 1-star and 2-star reviews followed by a demand for money, goods or services to remove them.

Google says not to engage with or pay the people involved, because it can encourage further attempts and doesn't guarantee the reviews are removed, and not to try to resolve it yourself by offering money or services.

Google asks owners to gather evidence right away and report through its merchant extortion form, including screenshots of the demands with dates, times and the sender's contact details, plus direct links to the suspicious reviews.
After a report, Google investigates and tells the owner the result, but says it can't share specific details of the investigation.
The extortion form is only for cases with a direct demand for money or favors. Spam or off-topic reviews go through Google's normal review reporting.

ol: Don't reply to the demand, and don't pay or offer anything.
Screenshot every message (email, WhatsApp, Telegram, social media or text) so the date, time and sender details show.
Copy the link to each suspicious review into one note or document, and write down when the reviews started and when the demand arrived.
Open Google's merchant extortion report form, fill in your business details, describe the reviews and the demand, attach the screenshots and submit.
Tell your staff, so nobody answers the scammer or offers a refund to make it stop.
Keep collecting real reviews the usual way (ask every customer, no incentives), and keep a copy of everything you submitted.

ul: A message offering to "fix" or remove your bad reviews for a fee can be part of the same scam, even if it sounds like a helpful service.
Don't reply to the fake reviews with accusations or customer details. Keep any public reply short and calm, or wait for Google's decision.

pages.seoTitle: Card testing fraud alert for small online stores (failed payment spike automation)
pages.summary: Card testing is when fraudsters use a store's checkout to find out which stolen card numbers still work, usually with lots of small payments or card setups. Stripe's docs say it can lead to disputes, higher decline rates and fees for the store. This recipe watches your failed payments and alerts you within minutes when they spike, so you can refund fraudulent charges and ask your developer or platform to tighten checkout before the damage grows.
steps: Pick your signal: failed or declined payments from your payment processor. Most processors and store platforms can send an event or email for each failed payment, and automation tools like Zapier, Make or n8n can receive them.
Have the automation add each failed payment to a Google Sheet with the time, amount, customer name and email.
Count failures in a rolling window, such as the last hour. Set a threshold well above your normal day (for example, three times your usual hourly failures), based on a few weeks of your own data.
When the count passes the threshold, text and email the owner and whoever manages the website: "Possible card testing: X failed payments in the last hour."
Include a quick look at the pattern Stripe describes: many low-amount payments, nonsense or random-looking names and emails, and lots of generic declines.

Open a short checklist in the alert: review recent successful small payments and refund the ones that look fraudulent, then ask your developer or platform about CAPTCHA, rate limits and guest checkout limits on the checkout.

p: Tools: your payment processor or store platform, a Google Sheet, and Zapier, Make or n8n for the counting and alerts. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page. If your processor offers built-in fraud rules (Stripe calls its tool Radar, and custom rules depend on your plan), check those first.

ul: Card testing is when fraudsters try to validate stolen card details by making many small payments or card setups on a business's site.
Signs include a sudden increase in failed or blocked payments, many declines with a generic decline reason, and low-amount payments using random or meaningless names and email addresses.
Card testing can result in disputes, higher decline rates and fees for the business.
Stripe recommends refunding payments that you believe are fraudulent, to help avoid disputes later.

Stripe's recommended checkout integrations include protections such as CAPTCHA and rate limiting, and its docs also suggest adding your own rate limits, limiting guest checkout where it makes sense, keeping secret API keys private and avoiding excessive payment retries.
Don't email or call the names on the fake orders. They're usually random, or belong to the real cardholders, who aren't the attackers.
Refunds and checkout changes are a person's decision. The automation only alerts and gathers the evidence.
If you're not technical, forward the Stripe page below to your web developer or store platform's support and ask what protections are already on.
Your processor may limit or pause your account if card testing continues, so treat an alert as urgent, even late at night.
